title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Vous pouvez m'aider + , + s'il vous plaît?
Il y a un problème avec + le/la + N

rules.text: avoir mal à is the fourth member of a family the learner has had since L1-M9. j'ai faim, j'ai froid, j'ai soif — and now j'ai mal à la tête. French treats a state as something you HAVE, and the article stands where English wants a possessive: à la tête, never à ma tête.

m'aider is ONE key to the index. The elision fuses the pronoun to what follows, so m'aider and t'aider are single surfaces rather than two words each. A learner who met me in front of a verb at M5 will look for it here and not find it — it is inside the next word.

The past here is L1-M5's passé composé and nothing more: J'ai perdu mon billet, J'ai oublié mon téléphone, Le train est parti. No plus-que-parfait, no subjunctive, and no conditional beyond M1's frozen je voudrais — which is why a complaint here is framed rather than hedged.

COMPLAINING CALMLY IS NOT HEDGING. The softening comes from the opening — Excusez-moi, il y a un problème… — and from Malheureusement. Directness about the fault itself is normal and is not rude; an English speaker's "there seems to be a slight issue" reads as evasive rather than as polite.

ça marche is M6's row doing its literal job. There it settled a plan; here it says a machine works, and Ça ne marche pas is the ordinary way to report a fault. One word, two readings, and the situation decides.

words.note: The one hedge French uses in a complaint. It reports regret about a fact; it does not weaken the fact itself.

sentences.trap: The politeness is entirely in Excusez-moi, and what follows is flat. Softening the fault as well is what makes an English speaker sound evasive here.
sentences.sound: ex-kü-zay-MWA sa nuh MARSH pa. The ne is barely sounded even when it is written.

variations.changed: without the opener — abrupt, but not rude
with the one hedge the language uses

mistake.display: Excusez-moi, il semble qu'il y a un petit problème
mistake.why: French states it: Excusez-moi, ça ne marche pas.

sentences.usage: Reporting a fault at a desk, a shop or a hotel.

words.note: The participle of perdre. With avoir it does not agree with anything, which M10 will state as a rule.
Both jobs on one word. The ill is the soft y of fille, and the final t is silent.

sentences.trap: The possessive IS used here, unlike in M2's feature frame. mon billet is a thing you own; la tête in the next sentence is part of you, and French treats the two differently.
sentences.sound: zhay per-DÜ mon bee-YEH. j'ai is one syllable.

mistake.why: With avoir the participle does not agree: J'ai perdu mon billet.

sentences.usage: At a station, a hotel desk, a lost-property office.
sentences.mnemonic: A thing you own keeps its possessive.

words.note: In j'ai mal it is the pain; on its own it is the adverb "badly" — Ça va mal. One word, and no later row can take it back.
The circumflex is a letter. It marks an s that used to be there — the English "test" and the French tête are cousins.

sentences.trap: This is the same avoir the learner has been using since L1-M9's j'ai faim. It is the fourth member of a family, not a new idiom — and the article, not a possessive, is what follows à.
sentences.sound: zhay mal a la TET. The circumflex e is open and long.

variations.changed: a masculine part, so à contracts to au

variations.display: Tu as mal à la tête?

variations.changed: plural, so à contracts to aux

mistake.why: The article does the work: J'ai mal à la tête.

sentences.usage: At a chemist's, or as a reason for going home.
sentences.mnemonic: The fourth member of the j'ai faim family.

words.note: The s is silent, and its plural is also dos. au dos, because it is masculine and à plus le fuses — with les it fuses to aux, as in aux pieds.

sentences.trap: au is à plus le, welded, and aux is à plus les. The frame does not change — only the article inside it does, and the gender of the body part decides.
sentences.sound: zhay mal o DO. Both o's are closed and neither final consonant is heard.

mistake.why: à and le fuse: J'ai mal au dos.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you cannot carry something.
sentences.mnemonic: à + le = au, à + les = aux.

sentences.display: Vous pouvez m'aider, s'il vous plaît?

words.note: ONE word: me plus aider, fused by the elision. The pronoun is still in front of its verb — it has simply been welded on.
M1 opened this row; here it is the bare infinitive beside the fused form. Both are index keys and neither answers for the other.
The noun and the verb cell are spelled the same. À l'aide! is the shout, and it is rarer than the English "help!"

sentences.trap: The pronoun has not moved — it has fused. m'aider is one token to the index and one word to the ear, and looking for a separate me is what confuses a learner here.
sentences.sound: voo poo-VAY may-DAY seel voo PLEH. The m' runs straight into the vowel.

variations.changed: the offer, where no elision happens

mistake.display: Vous pouvez me aider, s'il vous plaît?
mistake.why: The elision is compulsory: Vous pouvez m'aider, s'il vous plaît?

sentences.usage: Asking a stranger for real help.
sentences.mnemonic: The pronoun fuses, it does not move.

sentences.display: Il y a un problème avec la clé
sentences.cue: There's a problem with the key
sentences.literal: It there has a problem with the key

words.note: Masculine, despite the -e ending. The grave accent is a letter and the word is said pro-BLEM.
Feminine. It is also spelled clef, with a silent f, and both are current — this course writes clé.

sentences.trap: L1-M7's il y a is doing the work, and the il means nothing at all. It is the same placeholder as in il faut and il pleut.
sentences.sound: eel ya un pro-BLEM a-VEK la KLAY. The il y a runs together as two syllables.

variations.changed: negated, and M5's rule flattens the article

sentences.usage: The opening of any complaint at a desk.

sentences.display: J'ai oublié mon téléphone à la maison
sentences.cue: I've left my phone at home
sentences.literal: I-have forgotten my telephone at the house

words.note: French uses "forget" where English says "leave". laisser exists and means deliberately left, so the choice records whether it was an accident.
Two accented e's and both are sounded. The stress in French falls on the phrase rather than the word.

sentences.trap: English chooses between "forgot" and "left" by whether it was deliberate, and so does French — but the two languages draw the line in different places. An accident is always oublier.
sentences.sound: zhay oo-blee-AY mon tay-lay-FON. The oublié is four syllables.

variations.display: J'ai laissé mon téléphone à la maison
variations.cue: I left my phone at home

mistake.display: J'ai laissé mon téléphone à la maison par accident
mistake.why: An accident takes oublier: J'ai oublié mon téléphone à la maison.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you cannot show a ticket or answer a call.

words.note: The participle of L1-M6's partir. It takes être because it is movement, and then it AGREES with the subject — which a participle after avoir never does.
The participle of casser, used as an adjective. C'est cassé says a thing is broken without saying who broke it, which keeps a complaint calm.

sentences.trap: The auxiliary is est and not a, because partir is movement — and the participle then agrees with the train. M10 writes the rule down; here it is used.
sentences.sound: luh tran eh par-TEE. The an of train is nasal.

variations.display: Le train est parti à sept heures

variations.changed: a state rather than a movement, and it agrees

mistake.why: Movement takes être: Le train est parti.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you are late, or why a plan has failed.

words.note: M6's row, in its literal job. Ça marche settles a plan there; here Ça ne marche pas reports a machine that has stopped.

sentences.trap: Malheureusement is six syllables and does the work of one English word. It is the only softener a French complaint uses, and it goes at the front.
sentences.sound: mal-uh-ruh-zuh-MAHN. The h is silent and the whole word runs to a nasal ending.

variations.changed: a fault rather than a loss

mistake.why: The hedge goes at the front: Malheureusement, j'ai perdu ma clé.

sentences.usage: Delivering bad news, at a desk or on a phone.
sentences.mnemonic: One softener, and it goes first.

sentences.display: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la chambre
sentences.cue: Excuse me, there's a problem with the room
sentences.literal: Excuse-me, it there has a problem with the room

words.note: A bedroom or a hotel room. A room in general is une pièce, and une salle is a hall — three words where English has one.

sentences.trap: The complaint is stated flatly after the opener, and that is the whole technique. An English speaker's instinct is to bury the fault in qualifiers, and in French that reads as shifty rather than as polite.
sentences.sound: eel ya un pro-BLEM a-VEK la SHAHMBR. The ch is a sh.
